P25bs: They also need skills they can take with them, people outside, their own records, and somewhere to go next. If the community can help with the move, great. If it can't, it can still avoid punishing anyone for leaving, or holding back what they need. No upbringing is perfectly free. The point is to not turn belonging into a trap.
P21: I also searched the research corpus I've gathered for a single well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, with a good record of the whole sequence: what they did, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I failed to find one. Maybe the records are private, or the cases were sent somewhere else. Either way, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own, and the child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
P27: Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split apart over how to raise children. So how does a community of twenty adults, with twenty different childhoods, deal with screen time, vaccinations, schooling, religion, diet, discipline and medical care?
P28: This can't be settled on goodwill alone once a child is already living inside the disagreement. There must be sufficient agreement on principles about children for the community to be coherent, and enough freedom for parents to parent.
